source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)

books.section: The Railroads and Developments in the West

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which federal government policy promoted the economic development of the American West between 1862 and 1890.

documents.title: The Homestead Act
documents.source: Homestead Act of 1862, Sections 1-2. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress offering public land to settlers; the government's main tool for peopling the Plains with farmers.
documents.text:
"That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States, or who shall have filed his declaration of intention to become such, ... shall ... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands..."

"And upon filing the said affidavit with the register or receiver, and on payment of ten dollars, he or she shall thereupon be permitted to enter the quantity of land specified: Provided, however, That no certificate shall be given or patent issued therefor until the expiration of five years from the date of such entry."

documents.title: The Pacific Railway Act
documents.source: Pacific Railway Act of 1862, Section 3. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress subsidizing the transcontinental railroad; shows the government paying for construction with public land.
documents.text: "That there be, and is hereby, granted to the said company, for the purpose of aiding in the construction of said railroad and telegraph line, and to secure the safe and speedy transportation of the mails, troops, munitions of war, and public stores thereon, every alternate section of public land, designated by odd numbers, to the amount of five alternate sections per mile on each side of said railroad..."

documents.title: The Morrill Land-Grant Act
documents.source: Morrill Land-Grant Act of 1862, Section 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress granting public land to the states for colleges; shows the government using land to build agricultural knowledge.
documents.text: "That there be granted to the several States, for the purposes hereinafter mentioned, an amount of public land, to be apportioned to each State a quantity equal to thirty thousand acres for each senator and representative in Congress to which the States are respectively entitled by the apportionment under the census of eighteen hundred and sixty."

documents.title: Mark Twain on Virginia City
documents.source: Mark Twain, Roughing It (1872), Chapter 52. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A journalist who lived in the mining town, describing its boom; shows what mineral wealth did for settlement.
documents.text:
"The year 1863 was perhaps the very top blossom and culmination of the 'flush times.' Virginia swarmed with men and vehicles to that degree that the place looked like a very hive... Speculation ran riot, and yet there was a world of substantial business going on, too."

"All along under the center of Virginia and Gold Hill, for a couple of miles, ran the great Comstock silver lode — a vein of ore from fifty to eighty feet thick between its solid walls of rock — a vein as wide as some of New York's streets."

documents.title: Munn v. Illinois
documents.source: Munn v. Illinois, 94 U.S. 113 (1877), opinion of Chief Justice Waite. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Supreme Court decision upholding state regulation of grain elevators; shows the government answering farmers' complaints about corporate power.
documents.text: "Property does become clothed with a public interest when used in a manner to make it of public consequence, and affect the community at large. When, therefore, one devotes his property to a use in which the public has an interest, he, in effect, grants to the public an interest in that use, and must submit to be controlled by the public for the common good, to the extent of the interest he has thus created."

documents.title: The Dawes Severalty Act
documents.source: Dawes Severalty Act of 1887, Section 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An act of Congress dividing reservations into individual allotments; shows federal policy toward Native peoples as part of opening the West.
documents.text:
"To each head of a family, one-quarter of a section; To each single person over eighteen years of age, one-eighth of a section; To each orphan child under eighteen years of age, one-eighth of a section; and To each other single person under eighteen years now living... one-sixteenth of a section..."

(Paraphrase of Section 5: the United States would hold each allotment in trust for twenty-five years, after which the owner would receive title and citizenship.)

documents.title: Who got the public land
documents.source: Land-grant figures: Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 8; homestead figures: 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 17.
documents.sourcing: A table of how the federal government disposed of western land, drawn from the course books.
documents.text:
| Recipient | Amount |
| Railroad companies, in land grants to finance construction | more than 175 million acres |
| Railroad companies, money earned from selling grant land | about $435 million |
| Homesteaders, land transferred into private hands by 1900 | 85 million acres, in 610,000 claims |
| Homesteaders who had given up their farms by 1900 | about two-thirds |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which federal policy promoted western economic development between 1862 and 1890, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of promotion does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Civil War's end freeing the government to turn west, the nation's industrial growth, or the earlier history of federal land policy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about federal policy and western development.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Timber Culture Act of 1873, the Desert Land Act of 1877, the Timber and Stone Act of 1878, or the opening of Oklahoma in 1889.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of promotion, showing that policy helped some groups while harming others, or explaining why the same policies produced different results for settlers, companies, and Native peoples.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1862 and 1890 federal policy did more than any other single force to drive the economic development of the West, giving away the land and the charters that built farms, railroads, and mines, though the same policies enriched corporations and dispossessed Native peoples.
Context: The Civil War ended with the federal government holding a vast public domain and a new appetite for national projects, while eastern industry demanded western grain, meat, and minerals.
Evidence: Documents 1-3 show the three great land laws of 1862, Homestead, Pacific Railway, and Morrill, all giving public land away to build settlement, transport, and knowledge. Document 4 shows the mining economy those policies unleashed at Virginia City. Document 5 shows the government answering the corporate power its own policies created, and Document 6 shows the same state power turned against Native landholding. Document 7 measures the scale: railroads took more than twice the land homesteaders did, and two-thirds of homesteaders failed.
Beyond the documents: The Timber Culture and Desert Land Acts enlarged homestead claims because 160 acres proved too small, and the 1889 Oklahoma land run opened Indian land to settlers.
Sourcing: The Homestead and Railway Acts show Congress's own purposes in its own words; Twain, a working journalist in Virginia City, shows the boom from inside; the Munn opinion shows the Court answering a farmers' movement.
Complexity: Promotion was real but uneven. The same land laws that settled families also made railroads the West's greatest landlords, and the same government that built the West broke the peoples who already lived there.
